pergunta: Can you list for me all the usa secretaries of education from the beginning of 2018 until the end of 2024? including short acting secretaries
resposta:
Here are the U.S. Secretaries of Education who held the office from **January 1, 2018** through **December 31, 2024**, including every short‑acting appointment.  Dates are taken from the official biographies on Wikipedia (and corroborated by news reports):

| # | Name | Type | Start Date | End Date | Notes |
|---|------|------|------------|----------|-------|
| 1 | **Betsy DeVos** | Full Secretary | February 7, 2017 | January 8, 2021 | Confirmed Feb 7, 2017; sworn in Jan 20, 2021; resigned Jan 7, 2021 (effective Jan 8) → covered all of 2018. |
| 2 | **Mitchell “Mick” Zais** | Acting Secretary | January 8, 2021 | January 20, 2021 | Assumed immediately after DeVos’s resignation; one‑day acting tenure. |
| 3 | **Phil Rosenfelt** | Acting Secretary | January 20, 2021 | March 2, 2021 | Returned to the post while Biden’s administration sought a nominee; acted under Biden. |
| 4 | **Miguel Cardona** | Full Secretary | March 2, 2021 | January 20, 2025 | Confirmed March 1, 2021; sworn in March 2, 2021; remained in office throughout 2021–2024. |

**Why these four?**

* **Betsy DeVos** – Nominated by Trump (Nov 23, 2016), confirmed Feb 7, 2017; served until Jan 8, 2021.  
* **Mick Zais** – Served as Deputy Secretary from May 17, 2018; became acting secretary after DeVos resigned (Jan 8, 2021).  
* **Phil Rosenfelt** – Acting secretary appointed by Biden (Jan 20, 2021 – Mar 2, 2021) while the formal nominee (Cardona) was being vetted.  
* **Miguel Cardona** – Biden’s nominee, confirmed Mar 1, 2021; took oath Mar 2, 2021; served until Jan 20, 2025 (covering the entirety of 2024).

No other cabinet appointments occurred between 2018 and 2024; the next acting secretary (Denise L. Carter) began in January 2025, which falls outside the requested window.

**Sources**

* [United States Secretary of Education – Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Secretary_of_Education) – lists Betsy DeVos (2017–2021) and Miguel Cardona (2021–2025).  
* [Betsy DeVos – Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Betsy_DeVos) – “In office: February 7, 2017 – January 8, 2021”.  
* [Mick Zais – Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mick_Zais) – “Acting United States Secretary of Education … January 8, 2021 – January 20, 2021”.  
* [Phil Rosenfelt – Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Phil_Rosenfelt) – “Acting United States Secretary of Education … January 20, 2021 – March 2, 2021”.  
* [Miguel Cardona – Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miguel_Cardona) – “In office: March 2, 2021 – January 20, 2025”.

The **United States secretary of education** is the head of the [United States Department of Education](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Department_of_Education "United States Department of Education"). The secretary serves as the principal advisor to the president of the United States, and the federal government, on policies, programs, and activities related to all education in the United States. As a member of the [Cabinet of the United States](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cabinet_of_the_United_States "Cabinet of the United States"), the secretary is sixteenth in the [line of succession](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_presidential_line_of_succession "United States presidential line of succession") to the [presidency](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/President_of_the_United_States "President of the United States").[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Secretary_of_Education#cite_note-2) Prior to its creation as an Executive Department, there was a non-Cabinet level position called the [United States commissioner of education](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Commissioner_of_Education "United States Commissioner of Education") who led the [United States Office of Education](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Office_of_Education "United States Office of Education").

The current secretary of education is [Linda McMahon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Linda_McMahon "Linda McMahon"), serving in this role under President [Donald Trump](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Donald_Trump "Donald Trump").[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Secretary_of_Education#cite_note-3)

## Function

The United States secretary of education is a member of the [president](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/President_of_the_United_States "President of the United States")'s [Cabinet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cabinet_of_the_United_States "Cabinet of the United States") and is the sixteenth in the [United States presidential line of succession](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_presidential_line_of_succession "United States presidential line of succession").[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Secretary_of_Education#cite_note-4) This secretary deals with federal influence over [education policy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Education_policy "Education policy"), and heads the United States Department of Education.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Secretary_of_Education#cite_note-5)

The secretary is advised by the [National Advisory Committee on Institutional Quality and Integrity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NACIQI "NACIQI"), an advisory committee, on "matters related to accreditation and to the eligibility and certification process for institutions of higher education."[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Secretary_of_Education#cite_note-6)

Prior to the creation of the Department of Education in 1979, Education was a division of the Department of Health, Education, and Welfare.

**Miguel Angel Cardona** (born July 11, 1975) is an American educator who served as the 12th [United States Secretary of Education](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Secretary_of_Education "United States Secretary of Education") under [President](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/President_of_the_United_States "President of the United States") [Joe Biden](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joe_Biden "Joe Biden") from March 2, 2021 to January 20, 2025. A member of the [Democratic Party](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Democratic_Party_(United_States) "Democratic Party (United States)"), he was confirmed by the [U.S. Senate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Senate "United States Senate") by a vote of 64–33 on March 1, 2021.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miguel_Cardona#cite_note-1) Cardona previously served as commissioner of the [Connecticut State Department of Education](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Connecticut_State_Department_of_Education "Connecticut State Department of Education") from 2019 to 2021.

A native of [Meriden, Connecticut](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Meriden,_Connecticut "Meriden, Connecticut"), Cardona began his career as a fourth-grade teacher at Israel Putnam Elementary School in Meriden. In 2003, at the age of twenty-seven, he was named principal of Meriden's Hanover School, making him the youngest principal in the state.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miguel_Cardona#cite_note-2)[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miguel_Cardona#cite_note-3)

## Early life and education

Miguel Cardona was born on July 11, 1975, in [Meriden, Connecticut](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Meriden,_Connecticut "Meriden, Connecticut"), to [Puerto Rican](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Puerto_Rican_people "Puerto Rican people") parents.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miguel_Cardona#cite_note-:2-4)[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miguel_Cardona#cite_note-5) Cardona grew up speaking Spanish as his [first language](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/First_language "First language") and started to learn English when entering [kindergarten](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kindergarten "Kindergarten").[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miguel_Cardona#cite_note-:0-6)[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miguel_Cardona#cite_note-7) His father is a retired police officer in Meriden.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miguel_Cardona#cite_note-:3-8) Cardona was raised in a [housing project](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Housing_project "Housing project") in Meriden and graduated from the [H.C. Wilcox Technical High School](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/H.C._Wilcox_Technical_High_School "H.C. Wilcox Technical High School"), where he was a part of the automotive studies program. He visits his Alma Mater frequently, recently being the guest speaker for the class of 2023.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miguel_Cardona#cite_note-9)[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miguel_Cardona#cite_note-csde-10)[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miguel_Cardona#cite_note-ctmirror.org-11)

Cardona earned a Bachelor of Science in education from [Central Connecticut State University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Central_Connecticut_State_University "Central Connecticut State University") in New Britain, CT in 1997. He obtained a Master of Science in bilingual and bicultural education at [University of Connecticut](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Connecticut "University of Connecticut") (UConn) in 2001. In 2004, he completed a professional [sixth year certification](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Educational_specialist "Educational specialist") at UConn where he earned a [doctor of education](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Doctor_of_Education "Doctor of Education") in 2011.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miguel_Cardona#cite_note-csde-10)[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miguel_Cardona#cite_note-:1-12)

Cardona's dissertation, titled *Sharpening the Focus of Political Will to Address Achievement Disparities*, studied the gaps between [English-language learners](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/English-language_learner "English-language learner") and their classmates.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miguel_Cardona#cite_note-:1-12)[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miguel_Cardona#cite_note-:0-6) His doctoral major advisor was Barry G. Sheckley and his associate advisor was Casey D. Cobb.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miguel_Cardona#cite_note-:1-12)

## Career

Cardona began his career as a fourth-grade teacher at Israel Putnam Elementary School in [Meriden, Connecticut](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Meriden,_Connecticut "Meriden, Connecticut"). In 2003, at Hanover Elementary School, he was promoted and made the youngest [principal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Head_teacher "Head teacher") in the state's history for ten years. From 2015 to 2019, Cardona served as assistant superintendent for teaching and learning in his home town.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miguel_Cardona#cite_note-13)[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miguel_Cardona#cite_note-14)

Cardona was also an adjunct professor of education in the University of Connecticut's Department of Educational Leadership.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miguel_Cardona#cite_note-15) During his career, he has focused on closing gaps between English-language learners and their peers.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miguel_Cardona#cite_note-:0-6)

In August 2019, Governor [Ned Lamont](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ned_Lamont "Ned Lamont") appointed Cardona as [commissioner of education](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Connecticut_State_Department_of_Education "Connecticut State Department of Education"); Cardona was the first Latino to hold the position.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miguel_Cardona#cite_note-csde-10)[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miguel_Cardona#cite_note-ctmirror.org-11) During his tenure, Cardona helped oversee state schools' response to the [COVID-19 pandemic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/COVID-19_pandemic_in_Connecticut "COVID-19 pandemic in Connecticut"), where he expressed concerns over the long-term mental health impacts of [remote education](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Remote_education "Remote education") on students.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miguel_Cardona#cite_note-:3-8)

## Secretary of Education (2021–2025)

### Nomination and confirmation

In December 2020, Cardona emerged as a candidate for [United States secretary of education](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Secretary_of_Education "United States Secretary of Education") in [Joe Biden's cabinet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cabinet_of_Joe_Biden "Cabinet of Joe Biden"). Biden began to lean toward Cardona over two other "high-profile" teachers' union leaders, [Lily Eskelsen García](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lily_Eskelsen_García "Lily Eskelsen García") and [Randi Weingarten](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randi_Weingarten "Randi Weingarten"). By choosing Cardona over the two, Biden "appeared to have sidestepped any sibling rivalry between the [NEA](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Education_Association "National Education Association") and [AFT.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_Federation_of_Teachers "American Federation of Teachers")"[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miguel_Cardona#cite_note-16)[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miguel_Cardona#cite_note-17)

[![](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/9/9b/P20210805CS-0453_%2851478523057%29.jpg/250px-P20210805CS-0453_%2851478523057%29.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:P20210805CS-0453_(51478523057).jpg)Cardona talks with reporters during a press briefing on August 5, 2021, at the White House.

Cardona was brought to the attention of Biden by [Linda Darling-Hammond](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Linda_Darling-Hammond "Linda Darling-Hammond"), the leader of the transition's education secretary search efforts, a role she also filled for [Barack Obama](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Barack_Obama "Barack Obama") in 2008. Darling-Hammond and Cardona had worked together on numerous projects.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miguel_Cardona#cite_note-ctmirror.org-11) *[Politico](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Politico "Politico")* noted that "[Hispanic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hispanic "Hispanic") lawmakers are stressing in particular the need for a Latina to join the administration."[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miguel_Cardona#cite_note-18)

Cardona appeared before the [Senate Committee on Health, Education, Labor and Pensions](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Senate_Committee_on_Health,_Education,_Labor_and_Pensions "United States Senate Committee on Health, Education, Labor and Pensions") on February 3, 2021.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miguel_Cardona#cite_note-19) On February 25, his nomination was advanced by the Senate on a [cloture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cloture "Cloture") vote of 66–32.[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miguel_Cardona#cite_note-20) Cardona was confirmed on March 1, 2021, by a 64–33 vote. Cardona took his oath of office on March 1, 2021, and was ceremonially sworn in by Vice President [Kamala Harris](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kamala_Harris "Kamala Harris") on March 2, 2021.[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miguel_Cardona#cite_note-21)

### Tenure

[![](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/4/4d/The_Atlantic_Interview_with_Miguel_Cardona_on_14_December_2023_-_2.jpg/250px-The_Atlantic_Interview_with_Miguel_Cardona_on_14_December_2023_-_2.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:The_Atlantic_Interview_with_Miguel_Cardona_on_14_December_2023_-_2.jpg)Cardona speaks on a panel hosted by *[The Atlantic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Atlantic "The Atlantic")* in December 2023.

Throughout his tenure as Secretary of Education, Cardona was responsible for implementing several forms of forgiveness for [student loans](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Student_loans_in_the_United_States "Student loans in the United States").[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miguel_Cardona#cite_note-auto-22) The administration's most sweeping attempt to do so, which would have forgiven about $430 billion in student loan principles, was struck down by the [Supreme Court](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Supreme_Court_of_the_United_States "Supreme Court of the United States") on June 30, 2023, in *[Biden v. Nebraska](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Biden_v._Nebraska "Biden v. Nebraska")*.[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miguel_Cardona#cite_note-23) Following the *Biden v. Nebraska* decision, Cardona announced a series of smaller and more targeted student loan forgiveness programs, and the Department of Education has reemphasized the [Public Service Loan Forgiveness](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Public_Service_Loan_Forgiveness "Public Service Loan Forgiveness") program to reduce the student debt of people working full-time in [public service](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Public_service "Public service").[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miguel_Cardona#cite_note-auto-22)[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miguel_Cardona#cite_note-24)[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miguel_Cardona#cite_note-25) In December 2023, Cardona announced that the administration had forgiven about $132 billion of student debt in its first three years.[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miguel_Cardona#cite_note-auto-22) At President [Joe Biden](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joe_Biden "Joe Biden")’s [2024 State of The Union](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2024_State_of_the_Union_Address "2024 State of the Union Address"), Cardona was the [designated survivor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Designated_survivor "Designated survivor").[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miguel_Cardona#cite_note-26)

In December 2023, simplified [Free Application for Federal Student Aid](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Free_Application_for_Federal_Student_Aid "Free Application for Federal Student Aid") (FAFSA) forms were released after a two-month delay.[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miguel_Cardona#cite_note-27) By late March 2024, there was a backlog of 6 million applications.[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miguel_Cardona#cite_note-28) On April 26, the Education Department announced that the top official in charge of federal financial student aid would step down.[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miguel_Cardona#cite_note-29) Colleges across the country were obliged to delay their decision deadlines as students were still waiting for financial aid offers. On April 30, Cardona was questioned at a congressional hearing about the troubled introduction of the new form.[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miguel_Cardona#cite_note-30) On May 7, Cardona apologized at another congressional hearing.[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miguel_Cardona#cite_note-31)

## Personal life

In 2002, Cardona married Marissa Pérez, a [family-school liaison](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/School_social_worker "School social worker").[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miguel_Cardona#cite_note-Alverio-32) Pérez was named [Miss Connecticut](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miss_Connecticut "Miss Connecticut") in 2001 and [Miss Connecticut Teen USA](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miss_Connecticut_Teen_USA "Miss Connecticut Teen USA") in 1996.[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miguel_Cardona#cite_note-33)[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miguel_Cardona#cite_note-Alverio-32) Cardona and his wife have two children: a son, Miguel Jr., and a daughter, Celine.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miguel_Cardona#cite_note-csde-10) Cardona is [Catholic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Catholic_Church "Catholic Church").[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miguel_Cardona#cite_note-34)

## References

**Denise L. Carter**[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Denise_L._Carter#cite_note-1) is an American government official serving as the principal deputy chief operating officer for [Student Aid](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Federal_Student_Aid "Federal Student Aid") in the [United States Department of Education](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Department_of_Education "United States Department of Education").[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Denise_L._Carter#cite_note-:0-2) She served as the acting [United States secretary of education](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Secretary_of_Education "United States Secretary of Education") from January 20, 2025, until March 3, 2025.

## Career

Carter served in the [United States Department of Health and Human Services](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Department_of_Health_and_Human_Services "United States Department of Health and Human Services") in multiple roles, including as Deputy Assistant Secretary for Human Resources.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Denise_L._Carter#cite_note-3) She served as Acting Chief Operating Officer for [Student Aid](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Federal_Student_Aid "Federal Student Aid") from July 2024 until April 2025.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Denise_L._Carter#cite_note-:0-2)

Carter was appointed acting [United States secretary of education](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Secretary_of_Education "United States Secretary of Education") by President [Donald Trump](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Donald_Trump "Donald Trump") on January 20, 2025,[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Denise_L._Carter#cite_note-4) and was succeeded by Linda McMahon on March 3, 2025, following her confirmation by Congress.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Denise_L._Carter#cite_note-5)

Carter retired from the Department of Education on April 2, 2025.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Denise_L._Carter#cite_note-6)

**Mitchell McGeever** "**Mick**" **Zais** (born December 10, 1946) is an American education official and former general who served as the acting [United States secretary of education](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Secretary_of_Education "United States Secretary of Education").[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mick_Zais#cite_note-1) He previously served as the 17th [South Carolina Superintendent of Education](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Carolina_Superintendent_of_Education "South Carolina Superintendent of Education") from 2011 to 2015. Before winning the election as superintendent, he served as President of [Newberry College](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newberry_College "Newberry College") for ten years.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mick_Zais#cite_note-2) Prior to that he reached the rank of Brigadier General in the United States Army.

On January 7, 2021, Education Secretary [Betsy DeVos](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Betsy_DeVos "Betsy DeVos") submitted her resignation to the [President of the United States](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/President_of_the_United_States "President of the United States") because of the [2021 storming of the United States Capitol](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2021_storming_of_the_United_States_Capitol "2021 storming of the United States Capitol").[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mick_Zais#cite_note-3) As deputy secretary, Zais succeeded DeVos as [acting secretary](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Federal_Vacancies_Reform_Act_of_1998 "Federal Vacancies Reform Act of 1998").

## Early life and education

Zais was born in [Fort Bragg, North Carolina](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fort_Bragg,_North_Carolina "Fort Bragg, North Carolina").[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mick_Zais#cite_note-4) He earned a Bachelor of Science degree in engineering from [West Point](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/West_Point "West Point"), a Master of Science and a doctorate in social psychology and organizational behavior both from the [University of Washington](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Washington "University of Washington") and a Master of Arts in military history from the [School of Advanced Military Studies](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/School_of_Advanced_Military_Studies "School of Advanced Military Studies") at the [United States Army Command and General Staff College](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Army_Command_and_General_Staff_College "United States Army Command and General Staff College").

## Career

### Military

During his military career, Zais served in a wide variety of infantry units in [Vietnam](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vietnam "Vietnam"), the United States, and [Korea](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Korea "South Korea"). He commanded two rifle companies, an infantry battalion, a light infantry brigade, and served as deputy commanding general at [Fort Riley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fort_Riley "Fort Riley"), [Kansas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kansas "Kansas"). Zais was also the Pentagon's Chief of War Plans. As an assistant professor at West Point for three years, he taught organizational behavior, leadership, and management consulting.

Zais served as a White House aide and in Panama as executive assistant to the four-star commander of all U.S. forces in Central and South America. In Kuwait, he was commanding general of U.S. and Allied forces. He also served as commanding general of Operation Provide Refuge, the task force that cared for 4,000 Kosovo refugees who entered the United States. Zais's last military assignment was as Chief of Staff of the U.S. Army Reserve Command, the headquarters that administers the 184,000 part-time Reservists, 9,000 civilian employees, and 11,000 full-time military members of the Army Reserve. At the time of his retirement from the military Zais held the rank of Brigadier General.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mick_Zais#cite_note-5)

Zais's military awards and decorations include the Distinguished Service Medal; the Defense Superior Service Medal; the Legion of Merit; the Bronze Star; the Meritorious Service Medal; the Air Medal; the Republic of Vietnam Campaign Medal; the Humanitarian Service Medal; the Ranger, Airborne, and Combat Infantryman's Badges; and the South Carolina Meritorious Service Medal.

### Newberry College

Zais became the president of [Newberry College](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newberry_College "Newberry College") in August 2000. During his time at Newberry, both enrollment and endowment nearly doubled. During the last three years of his tenure, Newberry College was named by U.S. News & World Report as one of America's best colleges.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mick_Zais#cite_note-6) He retired in June 2010, just prior to running for state Superintendent of Education.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mick_Zais#cite_note-7)

### South Carolina Superintendent of Education

#### 2010 election

See also: [South Carolina elections, 2010 § Superintendent of Education](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Carolina_elections,_2010#Superintendent_of_Education "South Carolina elections, 2010")

Zais ran in a crowded field for the [Republican](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Republican_Party_(United_States) "Republican Party (United States)") nomination. Zais was the top vote getter in the primary but did not clear the necessary 50% threshold. Zais defeated Elizabeth Moffly in the run-off. He faced [Democrat](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Democratic_Party_(United_States) "Democratic Party (United States)") [Frank Holleman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Holleman "Frank Holleman"), [Libertarian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Libertarian "Libertarian") Tim Moultrie and two minor party candidates in the November general election. Zais won with 51% of the vote.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mick_Zais#cite_note-8)[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mick_Zais#cite_note-9)

#### Tenure and retirement

Zais opposed implementation of the [Common Core State Standards Initiative](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Common_Core_State_Standards_Initiative "Common Core State Standards Initiative") in South Carolina and withdrew from the state's participation in the federal [Race to the Top](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Race_to_the_Top "Race to the Top") grant competition. Zais supported the state's Governor to have the power to appoint the State Superintendent of Education, a position shared by a former Democratic Superintendent as well as his successor in the position.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mick_Zais#cite_note-10)[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mick_Zais#cite_note-11) By the end of Zais's tenure, South Carolina's on-time high school graduation rates hit an all-time high of over 80% of students finishing within four-years.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mick_Zais#cite_note-12) Zais decided not to run for re-election and endorsed [Sally Atwater](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Carolina_elections,_2014#Superintendent_of_Education "South Carolina elections, 2014"), widow of [Lee Atwater](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lee_Atwater "Lee Atwater"), as his replacement. In the 2014 election, Republican educator and former legislator, [Molly Mitchell Spearman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Molly_Mitchell_Spearman "Molly Mitchell Spearman"), won by a wide margin and replaced Zais as South Carolina's State Superintendent of Education.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mick_Zais#cite_note-13)

### U.S. Department of Education

On October 5, 2017, [President](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/President_of_the_United_States "President of the United States") [Donald Trump](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Donald_Trump "Donald Trump") announced his intention to nominate Zais to serve as the [United States Deputy Secretary of Education](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Deputy_Secretary_of_Education "United States Deputy Secretary of Education").[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mick_Zais#cite_note-14) He was confirmed by the [United States Senate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Senate "United States Senate") by a vote of 50–48 on May 16, 2018.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mick_Zais#cite_note-15)

After [Betsy DeVos](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Betsy_DeVos "Betsy DeVos") resigned as Secretary of Education on January 7, 2021, after the [storming of the United States Capitol](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2021_storming_of_the_United_States_Capitol "2021 storming of the United States Capitol"), Zais assumed the office of secretary on January 8. He remained in the position until January 20, 2021, when President [Joe Biden](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joe_Biden "Joe Biden") nominated [Phil Rosenfelt](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Phil_Rosenfelt "Phil Rosenfelt"), the former Acting General Counsel of the United States Department of Education, to serve in an acting capacity as Secretary of Education until [Miguel Cardona](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miguel_Cardona "Miguel Cardona"), the President's nominee, was confirmed by the Senate.

In June 2023, Zais endorsed [Tim Scott](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tim_Scott "Tim Scott") in the [2024 United States presidential election](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2024_United_States_presidential_election "2024 United States presidential election").[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mick_Zais#cite_note-16)In September 2025, Zais was named the government relations chair for the Boston 2026 World Expo.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mick_Zais#cite_note-17)

## Personal life

Zais has a daughter, Ashley, who was Miss South Carolina USA in 2007.[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mick_Zais#cite_note-18) His father, [Melvin Zais](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Melvin_Zais "Melvin Zais"), was a four-star general in the [United States Army](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Army "United States Army").[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mick_Zais#cite_note-19)

He served as president of the [American Philatelic Society](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_Philatelic_Society "American Philatelic Society") a non-profit organization focused on [philately](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Philately "Philately") or [stamp collecting](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stamp_collecting "Stamp collecting"), from August 2016 until his appointment as deputy secretary of education in May 2018.[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mick_Zais#cite_note-20) At the time he noted that with his role at the Department of Education he would "have to resign from all boards and all other employment."

**Philip H. Rosenfelt** is an American lawyer and civil servant who served as the acting [United States Secretary of Education](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Secretary_of_Education "United States Secretary of Education") from January 20, 2021 to March 2, 2021. He served in this same position under the [Trump administration](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/First_presidency_of_Donald_Trump "First presidency of Donald Trump") prior to the Senate confirming [Betsy DeVos](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Betsy_DeVos "Betsy DeVos").

On November 23, 2016, President-elect [Donald Trump](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Donald_Trump "Donald Trump") announced Betsy DeVos to be his designee for Secretary of Education.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Phil_Rosenfelt#cite_note-Buzzfeed_161123-1) Prior to DeVos' confirmation by the [United States Senate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Senate "United States Senate"), Rosenfelt was the acting Secretary of Education. Rosenfelt served from January 20, 2017 to February 7, 2017, when DeVos was sworn in.

With the departure of Betsy DeVos at the end of former president Donald Trump's term, Rosenfelt once again assumed the position of acting secretary; this time under the administration of President [Joe Biden](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joe_Biden "Joe Biden"). Rosenfelt was serving in an acting capacity under Joe Biden's administration until the Senate reviewed the nomination of [Miguel Cardona](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miguel_Cardona "Miguel Cardona") for the position.

## Personal life

Born in Paterson, New Jersey, Rosenfelt is of [Jewish descent](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jewish_descent "Jewish descent"). He received a bachelor of science degree from the [University of Pennsylvania](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Pennsylvania "University of Pennsylvania"), his juris doctor from [Columbia University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Columbia_University "Columbia University"), and his [LLM](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Master_of_Laws "Master of Laws") from [New York University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_York_University "New York University"). He began his service in the federal government in 1971 at the Department of Health, Education, and Welfare.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Phil_Rosenfelt#cite_note-2)

## Career

In 2005, Rosenfelt assumed the position of Deputy General Counsel of the United States Department of Education for Program Service. He served under the administration of [George W. Bush](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_W._Bush "George W. Bush"). He has continued to serve in that capacity since his appointment.

From January 20, 2017 to April 23, 2018, Rosenfelt served as the acting [General Counsel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/General_Counsel "General Counsel") of the [United States Department of Education](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Department_of_Education "United States Department of Education").

He has been designated as the acting [United States Secretary of Education](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Secretary_of_Education "United States Secretary of Education") on two occasions; the first of these from January 20, 2017 to February 7, 2017, and the second from January 20, 2021 until March 2, 2021. He has been replaced by [President Biden](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/President_Biden "President Biden")'s nominee [Miguel Cardona](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miguel_Cardona "Miguel Cardona") as he was confirmed by the Senate.

Currently, Rosenfelt serves as the Deputy General Counsel for Program Service in the Office of the General Counsel at the Department of Education.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Phil_Rosenfelt#cite_note-3)

**Elisabeth Dee DeVos** ([/dəˈvɒs/](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Help:IPA/English "Help:IPA/English") [*də-VOSS*](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Help:Pronunciation_respelling_key "Help:Pronunciation respelling key"); *née* **Prince**; born January 8, 1958) is an American politician, philanthropist, and former government official who served as the 11th [United States secretary of education](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Secretary_of_Education "United States Secretary of Education") from 2017 to 2021. DeVos is known for her [conservative](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conservative "Conservative") political activism,[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Betsy_DeVos#cite_note-mayer-dark-232-1) and particularly her support for [school choice](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/School_choice "School choice"), [school voucher](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/School_voucher "School voucher") programs, and [charter schools](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charter_school "Charter school").[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Betsy_DeVos#cite_note-2)[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Betsy_DeVos#cite_note-PulliamBailey-3)[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Betsy_DeVos#cite_note-Politico_120216-4)[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Betsy_DeVos#cite_note-Steward16-5) She was [Republican national committeewoman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Republican_National_Committee "Republican National Committee") for Michigan from 1992 to 1997 and served as chair of the [Michigan Republican Party](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michigan_Republican_Party "Michigan Republican Party") from 1996 to 2000, and again from 2003 to 2005. She has advocated for the Detroit charter school system[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Betsy_DeVos#cite_note-natreview_112816-6)[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Betsy_DeVos#cite_note-nytimes_062816-7) and she is a former member of the board of the [Foundation for Excellence in Education](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Foundation_for_Excellence_in_Education "Foundation for Excellence in Education"). She has served as chair of the board of the [Alliance for School Choice](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alliance_for_School_Choice "Alliance for School Choice") and the [Acton Institute](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Acton_Institute "Acton Institute") and headed the All Children Matter [PAC](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Political_action_committee "Political action committee").[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Betsy_DeVos#cite_note-8)

DeVos is married to former [Amway](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amway "Amway") CEO [Dick DeVos](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dick_DeVos "Dick DeVos").[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Betsy_DeVos#cite_note-9)[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Betsy_DeVos#cite_note-10) Her brother, [Erik Prince](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Erik_Prince "Erik Prince"), a former [U.S. Navy SEAL](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Navy_SEALs "United States Navy SEALs") officer, is the founder of [Blackwater USA](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Academi "Academi").[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Betsy_DeVos#cite_note-11)[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Betsy_DeVos#cite_note-investor_pleads_guilty_2016_03_16_foxnews-12)[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Betsy_DeVos#cite_note-strange_ascent_2018_10_vanity_fair-13) Their father is billionaire industrialist [Edgar Prince](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edgar_Prince "Edgar Prince"), founder of the Prince Corporation.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Betsy_DeVos#cite_note-investor_pleads_guilty_2016_03_16_foxnews-12)[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Betsy_DeVos#cite_note-strange_ascent_2018_10_vanity_fair-13)[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Betsy_DeVos#cite_note-Edgar_D._Prince-14)[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Betsy_DeVos#cite_note-15) In 2016, the family was listed by *[Forbes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Forbes "Forbes")* as the 88th-richest in America, with an estimated net worth of $5.4 billion.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Betsy_DeVos#cite_note-16)

On November 23, 2016, then-[president-elect](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/President-elect_of_the_United_States "President-elect of the United States") [Donald Trump](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Donald_Trump "Donald Trump") announced that he would nominate DeVos to serve as the secretary of education in his [administration](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/First_cabinet_of_Donald_Trump "First cabinet of Donald Trump").[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Betsy_DeVos#cite_note-Brown-17) On January 31, following strong opposition to the nomination from Democrats, the [Senate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Senate "United States Senate") [Committee on Health, Education, Labor and Pensions](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Senate_Committee_on_Health,_Education,_Labor_and_Pensions "United States Senate Committee on Health, Education, Labor and Pensions") approved her nomination on a party-line vote, sending her nomination to the Senate floor.[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Betsy_DeVos#cite_note-hill-committee-approves-18) On February 7, 2017, she was confirmed by the Senate by a 51–50 margin, with [Vice President](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vice_President_of_the_United_States "Vice President of the United States") [Mike Pence](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mike_Pence "Mike Pence") breaking the tie in favor of her nomination. This was the first time in U.S. history that a Cabinet nominee's confirmation was decided by the vice president's tiebreaking vote.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Betsy_DeVos#cite_note-19)[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Betsy_DeVos#cite_note-20)[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Betsy_DeVos#cite_note-21)

On January 7, 2021, DeVos tendered her resignation as education secretary as a result of the [January 6 United States Capitol attack](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/January_6_United_States_Capitol_attack "January 6 United States Capitol attack"), saying to President Trump in her resignation letter, "There is no mistaking the impact your rhetoric had on the situation."[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Betsy_DeVos#cite_note-22) Her resignation took effect on January 8, 2021, twelve days before the end of Trump's term.

## Early life

DeVos was born Elisabeth Prince on January 8, 1958. She grew up in [Holland, Michigan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Holland,_Michigan "Holland, Michigan"), the eldest of four children born to Elsa (Zwiep) Prince (later, Broekhuizen) and [Edgar Prince](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edgar_Prince "Edgar Prince"), a billionaire [industrialist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Business_magnate "Business magnate").[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Betsy_DeVos#cite_note-blackwater-23)[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Betsy_DeVos#cite_note-amway_heir-24) Edgar was the founder of Prince Corporation, an automobile parts supplier based in Holland, Michigan.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Betsy_DeVos#cite_note-Edgar_D._Prince-14)[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Betsy_DeVos#cite_note-blackwater-23) She is of [Dutch](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dutch_people "Dutch people") ancestry.[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Betsy_DeVos#cite_note-25)[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Betsy_DeVos#cite_note-Politico17-26)

DeVos was educated at the [Holland Christian High School](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Holland_Christian_Schools "Holland Christian Schools"), a private school located in her home town of Holland, Michigan.[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Betsy_DeVos#cite_note-newyorker-27) She graduated from [Calvin College](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Calvin_College "Calvin College") in [Grand Rapids, Michigan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grand_Rapids,_Michigan "Grand Rapids, Michigan"), where she earned a Bachelor of Arts degree in business economics in 1979.[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Betsy_DeVos#cite_note-28) During college, DeVos was involved with campus politics, volunteered for Gerald Ford's presidential campaign, and attended the 1976 [Republican National Convention](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Republican_National_Convention "Republican National Convention") to participate in a program for young Republicans.[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Betsy_DeVos#cite_note-Philanthropy-29)[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Betsy_DeVos#cite_note-Politico17-26)

DeVos grew up as a member of the [Christian Reformed Church in North America](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Christian_Reformed_Church_in_North_America "Christian Reformed Church in North America").[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Betsy_DeVos#cite_note-30) She has been a member and [elder](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elder_(Christianity) "Elder (Christianity)") of [Mars Hill Bible Church](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mars_Hill_Bible_Church "Mars Hill Bible Church") in Grand Rapids.[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Betsy_DeVos#cite_note-NewYorker2-31)[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Betsy_DeVos#cite_note-Haaretz1-32) Former [Fuller Seminary](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fuller_Seminary "Fuller Seminary") president [Richard Mouw](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Richard_Mouw "Richard Mouw"), with whom DeVos served on a committee, said she is influenced by [Dutch](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dutch_people "Dutch people") [neo-Calvinist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neo-Calvinism "Neo-Calvinism") theologian [Abraham Kuyper](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abraham_Kuyper "Abraham Kuyper"), a founding figure in [Christian Democracy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Christian_Democracy "Christian Democracy") political ideology.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Betsy_DeVos#cite_note-PulliamBailey-3)

## Political activity

[![](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/7/77/Laura_Bush_makes_a_purchase_at_Franklin_Cider_Mill_in_Franklin%2C_Mich.%2C_2006_%28cropped1%29.jpg/250px-Laura_Bush_makes_a_purchase_at_Franklin_Cider_Mill_in_Franklin%2C_Mich.%2C_2006_%28cropped1%29.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Laura_Bush_makes_a_purchase_at_Franklin_Cider_Mill_in_Franklin,_Mich.,_2006_(cropped1).jpg)DeVos (far left) is present as First Lady [Laura Bush](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Laura_Bush "Laura Bush") (far right) makes a purchase at [Franklin Cider Mill](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Franklin_Cider_Mill "Franklin Cider Mill"). Bush was in Michigan to support DeVos's husband in his gubernatorial campaign.

Since 1982, DeVos has participated in the [Michigan Republican Party](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michigan_Republican_Party "Michigan Republican Party"). She served as a local precinct delegate for the Michigan Republican Party, having been elected for 16 consecutive two-year terms since 1986.[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Betsy_DeVos#cite_note-33) She was a Republican National committeewoman for Michigan between 1992 and 1997,[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Betsy_DeVos#cite_note-34) and served as chairwoman of the Michigan Republican Party from 1996 to 2000.[[35]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Betsy_DeVos#cite_note-affirmative-35)[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Betsy_DeVos#cite_note-voters-36) In 2004, the *Lansing State Journal* described DeVos as "a political pit bull for most of (Democratic) Governor [[Jennifer] Granholm](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jennifer_Granholm "Jennifer Granholm")'s 16 months in office" and said that if DeVos was not Granholm's "worst nightmare", she was "certainly her most persistent".

[Bill Ballenger](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Ballenger "Bill Ballenger"), editor of the newsletter *Inside Michigan Politics* and a former Republican state senator, called DeVos "a good behind-the-scenes organizer and a good fund raiser" as well as "a true believer in core Republican issues that leave nobody in doubt on where she stands".[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Betsy_DeVos#cite_note-Charge-37) DeVos resigned the position in 2000. She said in that same year, "It is clear I have never been a rubber stamp. ... I have been a fighter for the grassroots, and following is admittedly not my strong suit."[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Betsy_DeVos#cite_note-Fresh-38) In 2003, DeVos ran again for party chairman and was elected to the post without opposition.[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Betsy_DeVos#cite_note-Fresh-38)

### Political fundraising

[![](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/b/bc/Betsy_DeVos_2005_crop.jpg/250px-Betsy_DeVos_2005_crop.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Betsy_DeVos_2005_crop.jpg)DeVos in 2005

DeVos personally raised more than $150,000 for the 2004 Bush re-election campaign,[[39]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Betsy_DeVos#cite_note-urges_bush-39) and hosted a Republican fundraiser at her home in October 2008 that was headlined by President [George W. Bush](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_W._Bush "George W. Bush").[[40]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Betsy_DeVos#cite_note-bush_attends-40) During the Bush administration she spent two years as the finance chairperson for the National Republican Senatorial Committee and worked closely with the administration on "various projects".[[41]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Betsy_DeVos#cite_note-Gathering-41) The DeVos family has been active in Republican politics for decades, particularly as donors to candidates and the party, giving more than $17 million to political candidates and committees since 1989.[[42]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Betsy_DeVos#cite_note-MLive-42)[[43]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Betsy_DeVos#cite_note-SmithGuardian-43)

#### Opposition to limits on political spending

Like other members of the DeVos family, Betsy strongly opposed government limits on political donations and spending. While popular with the American public[[44]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Betsy_DeVos#cite_note-JONES-pew-2018-44) as a way to prevent (perceived) unfair domination by the wealthy in politics, DeVos and many other conservatives argue it is an infringement on free speech. In a 1997 op-ed for *[Roll Call](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roll_Call "Roll Call")*, defending unlimited donations of "soft money" in political spending, DeVos compared government limits to [Big Brother](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Big_Brother_(Nineteen_Eighty-Four) "Big Brother (Nineteen Eighty-Four)") of [George Orwell](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Orwell "George Orwell")'s *[Nineteen Eighty-Four](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nineteen_Eighty-Four "Nineteen Eighty-Four")*.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Betsy_DeVos#cite_note-mayer-dark-232-1) Betsy was a founding board member of the [James Madison Center for Free Speech](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Madison_Center_for_Free_Speech "James Madison Center for Free Speech") which the DeVos family funded and whose "sole goal was to end all legal restrictions on money in politics".[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Betsy_DeVos#cite_note-mayer-dark-232-1)

She also wrote (in *Roll Call*) that she expected results from her political contributions. "My family is the largest single contributor of soft money to the national Republican Party. I have decided to stop taking offense at the suggestion that we are buying influence," she wrote. "Now I simply concede the point. They are right."[[45]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Betsy_DeVos#cite_note-Atlantic1-45)[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Betsy_DeVos#cite_note-Politico17-26) She also stated in the op-ed, "We expect to foster a conservative governing philosophy consisting of limited government and respect for traditional American virtues. … We expect a return on our investment; we expect a good and honest government. Furthermore, we expect the Republican Party to use the money to promote these policies and, yes, to win elections."[[46]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Betsy_DeVos#cite_note-ABC1-46)

### 2016 U.S. presidential election

During the [Republican Party presidential primaries for the 2016 election](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Republican_Party_presidential_primaries,_2016 "Republican Party presidential primaries, 2016"), DeVos initially donated to [Jeb Bush](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jeb_Bush "Jeb Bush") and [Carly Fiorina](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carly_Fiorina "Carly Fiorina") before eventually supporting [Marco Rubio](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marco_Rubio "Marco Rubio"). In March 2016, DeVos described Donald Trump as an "interloper" and said that he "does not represent the Republican Party".[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Betsy_DeVos#cite_note-Brown-17)

## Business career

DeVos is chairwoman of the [Windquest Group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dick_DeVos#The_Windquest_Group "Dick DeVos"), a privately held operating group that invests in technology, manufacturing, and [clean energy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sustainable_energy "Sustainable energy"). DeVos and her husband founded it in 1989.[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Betsy_DeVos#cite_note-Philanthropy-29) With a commitment of $100 million, Betsy DeVos's family was one of the largest investors—and losers—in blood-testing company [Theranos](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Theranos "Theranos").[[47]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Betsy_DeVos#cite_note-47)

DeVos and her husband were producers for a [Broadway](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Broadway_theatre "Broadway theatre") run of the stage play *[Scandalous: The Life and Trials of Aimee Semple McPherson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scandalous:_The_Life_and_Trials_of_Aimee_Semple_McPherson "Scandalous: The Life and Trials of Aimee Semple McPherson")*, in 2012, based on the life of [the famous evangelist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aimee_Semple_McPherson "Aimee Semple McPherson") and featuring a book and lyrics written by [Kathie Lee Gifford](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kathie_Lee_Gifford "Kathie Lee Gifford"). The show ran for three weeks, closing in December 2012[[48]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Betsy_DeVos#cite_note-48) after receiving negative reviews.[[49]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Betsy_DeVos#cite_note-49)[[50]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Betsy_DeVos#cite_note-50)

### Neurocore

Betsy and her husband Dick are chief investors in and board members of Neurocore, a group of brain performance centers offering [biofeedback](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Biofeedback "Biofeedback") therapy for disorders such as depression, attention deficit disorder, autism, and anxiety.[[51]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Betsy_DeVos#cite_note-NYT_Neurocore-51)[[52]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Betsy_DeVos#cite_note-WaPo_Neurocore2-52)[[53]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Betsy_DeVos#cite_note-Spectrum_Neurocore-53) The therapy consists of showing movies to patients and interrupting them when they become distracted, in an effort to retrain their brains. According to *[The New York Times](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_New_York_Times "The New York Times")*, a review of Neurocore's claims and interviews with medical experts suggest that the company's conclusions are unproven and its methods questionable.[[51]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Betsy_DeVos#cite_note-NYT_Neurocore-51) Democratic senators raised concerns about a potential [conflict of interest](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conflict_of_interest "Conflict of interest") and questioned whether she and her family members would "benefit financially from actions" she could take as the U.S. Secretary of Education. DeVos announced that she would step down from the company's board but would retain her investment in the company, valued at $5 million to $25 million.[[51]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Betsy_DeVos#cite_note-NYT_Neurocore-51)[[54]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Betsy_DeVos#cite_note-NYT_Neurcore2-54)[[55]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Betsy_DeVos#cite_note-WaPo_Neurocore-55) In November 2019, [Truth In Advertising](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Truth_in_Advertising_(organization) "Truth in Advertising (organization)") filed complaints[[56]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Betsy_DeVos#cite_note-TINA-Neurocore-56) against Neurocore with the [Food and Drug Administration](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Food_and_Drug_Administration "Food and Drug Administration") for unapproved medical devices[[57]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Betsy_DeVos#cite_note-TINA-FDA-57) and the [Federal Trade Commission](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Federal_Trade_Commission "Federal Trade Commission") for deceptive marketing.[[58]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Betsy_DeVos#cite_note-TINA-FTC-58)

## U.S. Secretary of Education

### Nomination

On November 23, 2016, Trump's transition team announced DeVos as the nominee to be the next [secretary of education](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Secretary_of_Education "United States Secretary of Education"). Upon her nomination, DeVos said "I am honored to work with the President-elect on his vision to make American education great again. The *status quo* in ed is not acceptable."[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Betsy_DeVos#cite_note-Brown-17) DeVos's nomination was generally criticized by teachers' unions and praised by supporters of [school choice](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/School_choice "School choice").[[59]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Betsy_DeVos#cite_note-insider-59)

*[Detroit Free Press](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Detroit_Free_Press "Detroit Free Press")* editor Stephen Henderson expressed concerns over DeVos's nomination, writing that "DeVos isn't an educator, or an education leader".[[60]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Betsy_DeVos#cite_note-BBC_020517-60)[[61]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Betsy_DeVos#cite_note-DFP_120317-61) Rebecca Mead of *[The New Yorker](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_New_Yorker "The New Yorker")* questioned the efficacy of Michigan's charter school system, which DeVos has supported.[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Betsy_DeVos#cite_note-newyorker-27) [Randi Weingarten](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randi_Weingarten "Randi Weingarten"), president of the [American Federation of Teachers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_Federation_of_Teachers "American Federation of Teachers"), called DeVos "the most ideological, anti-public education nominee" since the position became a cabinet position.[[62]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Betsy_DeVos#cite_note-:0-62) The Michigan chapter of the [American Civil Liberties Union](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_Civil_Liberties_Union "American Civil Liberties Union") and the Michigan Democratic Party opposed DeVos's nomination.[[59]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Betsy_DeVos#cite_note-insider-59)

Former presidential candidates [Jeb Bush](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jeb_Bush "Jeb Bush") and [Mitt Romney](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mitt_Romney "Mitt Romney") respectively called DeVos an "outstanding pick" and a "smart choice".[[62]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Betsy_DeVos#cite_note-:0-62)[[63]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Betsy_DeVos#cite_note-WaPo_010917-63) Republican senator [Ben Sasse](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ben_Sasse "Ben Sasse") said DeVos "has made a career out of standing up to powerful and connected special interests on behalf of poor kids who are too often forgotten by Washington". In an opinion editorial, the *[Chicago Tribune](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chicago_Tribune "Chicago Tribune")* wrote that "DeVos has helped lead the national battle to expand education opportunities for children".[[64]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Betsy_DeVos#cite_note-64)

#### Debate and final vote

[https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/transcoded/6/68/Betsy_DeVos_final_confirmation_vote_in_US_Senate_tie_broken_by_Mike_Pence.webm/Betsy_DeVos_final_confirmation_vote_in_US_Senate_tie_broken_by_Mike_Pence.webm.240p.vp9.webm](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/transcoded/6/68/Betsy_DeVos_final_confirmation_vote_in_US_Senate_tie_broken_by_Mike_Pence.webm/Betsy_DeVos_final_confirmation_vote_in_US_Senate_tie_broken_by_Mike_Pence.webm.240p.vp9.webm)

Vice President Mike Pence breaks the 50–50 tie in favor of DeVos, confirming her as U.S. secretary of education.

On January 31, DeVos's nomination was approved by the committee on a 12–11 party-line vote and was due to be voted on by the Senate.[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Betsy_DeVos#cite_note-hill-committee-approves-18) Later on February 1, 2017, two Republican U.S. senators, [Susan Collins](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Susan_Collins_(politician) "Susan Collins (politician)") from [Maine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maine "Maine") and [Lisa Murkowski](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lisa_Murkowski "Lisa Murkowski") from [Alaska](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alaska "Alaska"), came out against the confirmation (despite supporting DeVos in committee when both of them voted to move her nomination to the floor),[[79]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Betsy_DeVos#cite_note-79) bringing the predicted confirmation vote on DeVos to 50–50 if all Democrats and independents voted as expected, meaning Vice President [Mike Pence](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mike_Pence "Mike Pence") would have to break the tie.[[80]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Betsy_DeVos#cite_note-hill-vote-80) During an unusually early 6:30 a.m. vote on February 3, 2017, [cloture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cloture "Cloture") was invoked on DeVos's nomination in the Senate, requiring a final vote on the confirmation to happen after 30 hours of debate.[[81]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Betsy_DeVos#cite_note-hill-cloture-81)

Ahead of the scheduled final vote at noon on February 7, 2017, the Democrats in the Senate continuously spoke on the floor against the confirmation of DeVos the entire night before leading up to the vote, in protest of their strong disapproval of the nominee.[[82]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Betsy_DeVos#cite_note-hill-protest-82) As expected, there was a 50–50 tie on the final vote, with all Democrats and independents, along with two Republicans ([Susan Collins](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Susan_Collins_(politician) "Susan Collins (politician)") and [Lisa Murkowski](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lisa_Murkowski "Lisa Murkowski")), voting in opposition to DeVos, while the other fifty Republican senators voted in support of the confirmation, including Senator [Jeff Sessions](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jeff_Sessions "Jeff Sessions"), who himself had been nominated by the Trump administration for the post of [United States attorney general](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Attorney_General "United States Attorney General"). Republicans scheduled Sessions's confirmation vote after DeVos's so that he would be able to cast his vote in support of DeVos. Had his confirmation vote been earlier than hers, he would have been forced to resign from the Senate, therefore losing a vital vote for the Republicans on the confirmation.[[83]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Betsy_DeVos#cite_note-83)[[84]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Betsy_DeVos#cite_note-84)[[85]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Betsy_DeVos#cite_note-85) Since there was a tie, [Vice President](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vice_President_of_the_United_States "Vice President of the United States") [Mike Pence](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mike_Pence "Mike Pence") had to step in to decide the vote as the [president of the Senate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/President_of_the_Senate "President of the Senate").[[86]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Betsy_DeVos#cite_note-86) He [cast his tie-breaking vote](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_tie-breaking_votes_cast_by_vice_presidents_of_the_United_States "List of tie-breaking votes cast by vice presidents of the United States") in favor of DeVos to officially confirm her as education secretary.[[87]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Betsy_DeVos#cite_note-nyt-confirm-87) This was the first tie decided by a vice president on any vote in the Senate since the [George W. Bush administration](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Presidency_of_George_W._Bush "Presidency of George W. Bush").[[88]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Betsy_DeVos#cite_note-88)[[89]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Betsy_DeVos#cite_note-89)

### Staffing

DeVos said that on the basis of her first few days in the job, she had concerns that some Education Department employees were sympathetic to the [Obama administration](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Obama_administration "Obama administration"). "I . . . would not be surprised if there are also those that would try to subvert the mission of this organization and this department," she stated. Asked what she could do about that, she said, "Whatever can be done will be done, and it will be done swiftly and surely."[[90]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Betsy_DeVos#cite_note-90)

In April 2017, DeVos praised the president's nomination of [Carlos G. Muñiz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carlos_G._Muñiz "Carlos G. Muñiz") as the department's [general counsel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/General_counsel "General counsel").[[91]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Betsy_DeVos#cite_note-91)

In April 2017, DeVos named [Candice Jackson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Candice_Jackson "Candice Jackson") Deputy Assistant Secretary in the department's [Office for Civil Rights](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Office_for_Civil_Rights "Office for Civil Rights"), where she will be acting assistant secretary while that higher, Senate-confirmed appointment is vacant.[[92]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Betsy_DeVos#cite_note-NYT3june17-92) DeVos named Jason Botel Deputy Assistant Secretary for Elementary and Secondary Education.[[92]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Betsy_DeVos#cite_note-NYT3june17-92) Botel, a registered Democrat who supported President Obama and the [Black Lives Matter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Black_Lives_Matter "Black Lives Matter") movement, founded the [KIPP](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/KIPP_(organization) "KIPP (organization)") Ujima Village Academy in [Baltimore](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Baltimore "Baltimore"), after working for [Teach For America](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Teach_For_America "Teach For America").[[92]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Betsy_DeVos#cite_note-NYT3june17-92)

In mid-May 2018, *The New York Times* reported that under DeVos, the size of the team investigating abuses and fraud by for-profit colleges was reduced from about twelve members under the Obama administration to three, with their task also being scaled back to "processing student loan forgiveness applications and looking at smaller compliance cases". DeVos also appointed Julian Schmoke as the team's new supervisor; Schmoke was a former dean of DeVry Education Group, which was one of the institutions the team had been investigating. The investigation into DeVry was not the only one stopped, others include those of Bridgepoint Education and Career Education Corporation. The Education Department has hired more ex-employees and people affiliated with those institutions, such as Robert S. Eitel, senior counselor to DeVos, Diane Auer Jones, an advisor to the department, and Carlos G. Muñiz, the department's general counsel.[[93]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Betsy_DeVos#cite_note-93)

In October 2018, it was announced that DeVos's chief of staff, Josh Venable, would be replaced by Nate Bailey, who at that time was DeVos's chief of communications.[[94]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Betsy_DeVos#cite_note-94) Two years later, Venable joined an anti-Trump group, the [Republican Political Alliance for Integrity and Reform](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Republican_Political_Alliance_for_Integrity_and_Reform "Republican Political Alliance for Integrity and Reform") (REPAIR), which is led by former White House officials.[[95]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Betsy_DeVos#cite_note-95)

### Policy actions

#### School choice and private schools

In February 2017, DeVos released a statement calling [historically black colleges](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Historically_black_colleges_and_universities "Historically black colleges and universities") "real pioneers when it comes to school choice", causing controversy as some pointed out the schools originated after segregation laws prevented African Americans from attending others. DeVos later acknowledged racism as an important factor in the history of historically black colleges.[[96]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Betsy_DeVos#cite_note-96)

On March 24, 2017, during a visit to the [Osceola County](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Osceola_County,_Florida "Osceola County, Florida") campus of [Valencia College](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Valencia_College "Valencia College"), DeVos said she was considering the extension of federal financial aid for students that were year-round and interested in placing more focus on community colleges.[[97]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Betsy_DeVos#cite_note-97)

DeVos delivered her first extended policy address on March 29, 2017, at the [Brookings Institution](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brookings_Institution "Brookings Institution") which included the topic of school choice which has been her main advocacy issue for more than 30 years.[[98]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Betsy_DeVos#cite_note-AP_2019-05-06-98) She stated an interest in implementing choice policies directed toward children as individuals and criticizing the Obama administration's additional funding of $7 billion for the U.S.'s worst-performing schools as "throwing money at the problem" in an attempt to find a solution.[[99]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Betsy_DeVos#cite_note-99) On May 22, 2017, DeVos announced the Trump administration was offering "the most ambitious expansion" of school choice within American history. DeVos cited [Indiana](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indiana "Indiana") (which has the U.S.'s largest [school voucher](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/School_voucher "School voucher") program) as a potential model for a nationwide policy but did not give specific proposals.[[100]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Betsy_DeVos#cite_note-100)

In a May 2017 House of Representatives committee hearing, Rep. [Katherine Clark](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Katherine_Clark "Katherine Clark"), said an Indiana private school which takes publicly funded vouchers maintains it is entitled to deny admission to LGBTQ students or those coming from families with "homosexual or bisexual activity." Clark asked if she would inform Indiana that it could not discriminate in that way if it accepted federal funding and asked her how she would respond in the event a voucher school rejected black students but a state "said it was okay." DeVos answered: "Well again, the Office of Civil Rights and our [Title IX protections](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Title_IX_protections "Title IX protections") are broadly applicable across the board, but when it comes to parents making choices on behalf of their students..." Clark stopped her saying, "This isn't about parents making choices, this is about the use of federal dollars. Is there any situation? Would you say to Indiana, that school cannot discriminate against LGBT students if you want to receive federal dollars? Or would you say the state has the flexibility?" DeVos responded: "I believe states should continue to have flexibility in putting together programs ..."[[101]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Betsy_DeVos#cite_note-Tribune-101)

CBS reporter [Lesley Stahl](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lesley_Stahl "Lesley Stahl") questioned DeVos, in a March 2018 *[60 Minutes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/60_Minutes "60 Minutes")* interview, about the documented failure of the DeVos programs to demonstrate a positive result, in Michigan, her home state: "Your argument that if you take funds away that the schools will get better is not working in Michigan ... where you had a huge impact and influence over the direction of the school system." Stahl added, "The public schools here are doing worse than they did." DeVos was unable to provide any actual examples of improvement, but stated there were "pockets" where schools had done better than public schools.[[102]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Betsy_DeVos#cite_note-102)

On June 6, 2017, DeVos said [states' rights](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/States'_rights "States' rights") would determine private schools being allocated funds by the federal government during an appearance before members of a House appropriations committee.[[103]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Betsy_DeVos#cite_note-103)

#### Student loans

On April 11, 2017, DeVos undid several Obama administration policy memos issued by [John King Jr.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_King_Jr. "John King Jr.") and Ted Mitchell which were designed to protect [student loan borrowers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Student_loans_in_the_United_States "Student loans in the United States").[[104]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Betsy_DeVos#cite_note-104)

On July 6, 2017, Democratic attorneys-general in 18 states and Washington, D.C., led by Massachusetts attorney-general [Maura Healey](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maura_Healey "Maura Healey"), filed a federal lawsuit against DeVos for suspending the implementation of rules that were meant to protect students attending for-profit colleges. The rules, developed during the Obama administration, were meant to take effect on July 1, 2017.[[105]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Betsy_DeVos#cite_note-105)[[106]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Betsy_DeVos#cite_note-guardian-6jul2017-106)

On September 12, 2018, DeVos lost the lawsuit brought by 19 states and the District of Columbia, which accused the Department of Education of improperly delaying implementation of regulations protecting student loan borrowers from predatory practices.[[107]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Betsy_DeVos#cite_note-107)

#### Coronavirus pandemic

During the [coronavirus pandemic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/COVID-19_pandemic_in_the_United_States "COVID-19 pandemic in the United States"), DeVos directed millions of dollars of coronavirus relief funds from the [Coronavirus Aid, Relief and Economic Security Act](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/CARES_Act "CARES Act") intended for public schools and colleges, to private and religious schools.[[108]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Betsy_DeVos#cite_note-108)

DeVos pushed for schools to re-open while coronavirus cases were still surging in large parts of the country. She said that the Trump administration was considering pulling funding from public schools unless they provided full-time in person learning during the pandemic.[[109]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Betsy_DeVos#cite_note-:1-109) On July 12, 2020, she said "there's nothing in the data that suggests that kids being in school is in any way dangerous to them", an assertion that public health experts disputed.[[109]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Betsy_DeVos#cite_note-:1-109) She also refused to say whether schools should follow guidelines laid out by the [Centers for Disease Control and Prevention](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Centers_for_Disease_Control_and_Prevention "Centers for Disease Control and Prevention") (CDC) on reopening schools.[[110]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Betsy_DeVos#cite_note-110)
